textbookText: Worked out Examples: 1. A roller coaster with a mass of 2500 kg has a speed of 10 ms-1 as it goes over a 13 m hill. When it reaches the crest of an 8 m hill, it is moving at 13 ms-1. How much work did friction do on the coaster?

Solution: Here, Mass, m = 2500 g Speed, vi=10 ms-1 Speed, vi = 13 ms-1 Height, hi = 13 m Height, hf = 10 m KEf +GPEf = KEi+ GPEi +Wf OR, mvf2 +mghf = 1/2mvi2 +mghi +Wf OR, 1/2×2500x169 + 2500×9.8x8 = 1/2×2500×100 +2500x9.8×13 +Wf ⇒Wf = -36250 joule Friction usually does perform negative work and it slows down them.

3. A body of mass 2 kg initially at rest moves under the action of an applied horizontal force of 7 N on a table with the coefficient of kinetic friction = 0.1. Compute the; (a) Work done by the applied force in 10 s. (b) Work done by friction in 10 s. (c) Work done by the net force on the body in 10 s. (d) Change in kinetic energy of the body in 10 s.

Solution: The mass of the body = 2 kg Horizontal force applied = 7 N Coefficient of kinetic friction = 0.1 Acceleration produced by the applied force, a1 = F/m = 7/2 = 3.5 ms-1 2 Force of friction, f = μR = μmg = 0.1 × 2 × 9.8 = 1.96 N
Retardation produced by friction, a2 = -f/m = -196/2 = -0.98 ms-1 2 Net acceleration with which the body moves, a = a1 + a2 = 3.5 – 0.98 = 2.52 ms-1 2
Distance moved by the body in 10 seconds,
(a) The time at which work has to be determined is t = 10 s
Work = Force × displacement
(b) Work done by the friction in 10 s

The work done by the net force is equal to the final kinetic energy.

5.8 Collision; Elastic and Inelastic Collision In physics, the term "collision" typically implies an interaction between two or more objects where they exert forces on each other, resulting in a change in their motion. While physical contact is the most common scenario in collisions, it is not strictly necessary for a collision to occur. For example, the collision of α-particles with the nucleus involves no physical contact, whereas the collision between two billiard balls or a cricket ball and a bat does.

Though most common examples of collisions involve physical contact, it is true that, in a broader sense, a collision can occur without direct physical contact if there is an interaction through forces such as gravitational or electromagnetic forces, leading to a change in motion. However, in everyday usage and most introductory physics contexts, collisions are typically associated with physical contact.
During a collision, the total energy and momentum of the system of colliding objects remain conserved.

Coefficient of Restitution For any two colliding bodies, the ratio of the relative velocity after the collision to the relative velocity before the collision is called the coefficient of restitution. i.e., Coefficient of Restitution, e = Relative velocity after collision/Relative velocity before collision.

The value of e lies as 0 <e <1, e = 1 for perfectly elastic collision. e = 0, for perfectly inelastic collision. 5.8.1Types of Collision Elastic Collision In an elastic collision, both the momentum and KE are conserved i.e, m1u1 +m2u2 = m1v1 +m2v2

Such collisions occur among atomic or subatomic particles, nuclear particles, and gaseous molecules, where there is no conversion of mechanical energy into sound, heat, or other forms of energy during the collision. Consequently, the forces involved are called conservative forces. When a ball on a billiard table hits another ball, it is often approximated as an elastic collision, although in reality, it is nearly but not perfectly elastic due to minor energy losses.
